chapters.title: Chapter 5: Owning Real Estate Without Buying Property

lessons.title: Fractional Ownership and SEBI's SM REIT Framework

children.text: In 2022, Neha, a 35-year-old product manager in Hyderabad, put ₹25 lakh into a slice of a pre-leased office building in Bengaluru through an online fractional ownership platform. The pitch was simple: Grade A office, a multinational tenant, around 8% to 9% rental yield. What she actually owned was a stake in a private company that owned the floors, and if she wanted out, she had to wait for the platform to find another buyer. Deals like hers grew into thousands of crores with little specific regulation. In 2024, SEBI brought them inside its rulebook as Small and Medium REITs. This lesson explains both.

body.text: Fractional ownership lets you own a piece of one building. SM REITs put that idea under SEBI regulation. The rent can be higher than a large REIT's, but so is the risk, because your money depends on one or two assets and often one tenant.

children.text: How Fractional Ownership Worked Before SEBI Stepped In

markDefs.definition: A model where many investors pool money to jointly own a single property, usually a pre-leased commercial asset, through a company or LLP set up to hold it.
A property that already has a tenant with a signed lease at the time you invest.

children.text: Platforms like Strata, hBits and Property Share popularised
in India. A platform would identify a

office or warehouse, set up a special purpose vehicle to buy it, and sell stakes in that vehicle to investors, typically with tickets of ₹10 lakh to ₹25 lakh. Investors received a share of the rent and paid the platform management fees. The model worked well while tenants paid, but it sat outside a dedicated regulatory framework: disclosure standards, valuation practices and exit routes varied from platform to platform.

children.text: The Income, and the Single-Tenant Risk

A projected 9% yield is attractive next to large REITs yielding roughly 5% to 7%. On ₹10 lakh, 9% is ₹90,000 a year before tax, or ₹22,500 a quarter. But a single-building scheme with a single tenant has no cushion. If that tenant leaves at a lease break, the scheme's rent can fall to almost nothing until a new tenant is found, while property tax and maintenance keep running.

body.title: Quarterly income
body.prompt: You invest the ₹10 lakh minimum in an SM REIT scheme with a projected distribution yield of 9% a year, paid quarterly. Assuming the projection holds, how much would you receive each quarter before tax, in ₹?
body.explanation: ₹10,00,000 × 9% = ₹90,000 a year. ₹90,000 ÷ 4 = ₹22,500 a quarter. Remember that this is a projection based on the current lease, not a guaranteed payout.

body.title: When the only tenant leaves
body.prompt: An SM REIT scheme yields 9% a year while leased. Its only tenant leaves, and the building stays empty for 8 months of the year before a new tenant signs. Ignoring ongoing costs, what is the scheme's effective yield for that year, in %?
body.explanation: Rent is earned for only 4 of 12 months: 9% × 4 ÷ 12 = 3%. After property tax and maintenance on the empty floors, it would be even lower. That is the price of concentration, the same lesson as the single strata office in Chapter 2.

body.value: Tenant strength, lock-in period and years left on the lease
body.context: A 9-year lease is only as secure as its lock-in and the tenant's financial health. Read when the tenant can exit, what rent escalations apply, and how much of the scheme's income depends on each tenant.

body.text: Not every "fractional ownership" offer is an SM REIT. Some structures, especially for holiday homes, villas or small assets, may sit outside the SM REIT framework entirely. Before investing, confirm whether the product is a registered SM REIT scheme managed by a SEBI-registered investment manager. If it is not, you do not get SM REIT protections, whatever the marketing says.

Treat SM REIT schemes like individual stocks rather than like an index fund. One scheme is a concentrated bet on one building and one tenant. If you like the asset class, spreading money across several schemes, or combining them with large listed REITs, gives you the higher yield without resting everything on a single lease.

body.title: The biggest risk
body.question: An SM REIT scheme owns four floors of one Pune office building, leased to one IT company with a lock-in ending in 18 months. What is the biggest specific risk for an investor?
options: The scheme is not regulated by SEBI
The tenant may leave after the lock-in, cutting the scheme's income sharply
The minimum investment is only ₹10 lakh
Units can never be sold under any circumstances
body.explanation: SM REIT schemes are SEBI-regulated and listed, but a single building with one tenant means income depends entirely on that lease. A lock-in ending in 18 months is the key date to watch: after it, the tenant can exit and income could fall steeply until the space is re-let.

body.title: Dr Kiran's ₹30 lakh
body.scenario: Dr Kiran, a 42-year-old surgeon in Kochi, has ₹30 lakh to invest for regular income. He is considering putting all ₹30 lakh into one SM REIT scheme projecting a 9.2% yield from a single Grade A office in Hyderabad leased to a global bank. A friend suggests large listed REITs at around 6% instead.
body.prompt: How should he think about the choice?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Income gap: 9.2% on ₹30 lakh is about ₹2.76 lakh a year; 6% is ₹1.8 lakh. The extra ₹96,000 a year is compensation for concentration risk.
2. Lease details: he should check the lock-in expiry, years left on the lease, rent escalations and whether the bank's lease allows early exit.
3. Single-tenant risk: if the bank leaves after its lock-in, income could fall to near zero until the space is re-let. Large REITs spread this risk across hundreds of tenants.
4. Liquidity: SM REIT units may trade thinly, so selling quickly at a fair price may be hard. Large REIT units trade actively.
5. Fees and valuation: he should compare the issue price with the independent valuation and understand the manager's fees.
6. A balanced approach: rather than all ₹30 lakh in one scheme, he could split between two or three SM REIT schemes with different tenants and cities, and large listed REITs. That keeps a good share of the higher yield while limiting damage from any single tenant leaving.
7. Tax: he should check how distributions are taxed at his slab before comparing headline yields.

body.title: Before Investing in an SM REIT Scheme
steps: Confirm the scheme and its investment manager are registered with SEBI
Identify the tenant, its credit strength and its share of the scheme's rent
Read the lease: tenure, lock-in expiry, escalations and exit clauses
Compare the projected yield with large listed REITs and ask what the extra yield is paying for
Check the independent valuation against the issue price
Understand all management and other fees
Check how actively the units trade before counting on a quick exit
Limit how much of your portfolio sits in any single scheme

points: Fractional ownership platforms let investors pool money into single pre-leased buildings, largely outside a dedicated regulatory framework.
SEBI's SM REIT framework, introduced in March 2024, regulates schemes holding assets of ₹50 crore to under ₹500 crore, with a ₹10 lakh minimum.
SM REIT schemes must keep at least 95% of assets in completed, rent-generating property and list their units on an exchange.
PropShare Platina, India's first SM REIT scheme, offered a projected 9% yield from floors leased to a single tenant.
Higher projected yields come with single-building, single-tenant risk and potentially thin trading.
Check SEBI registration, the tenant, the lock-in and valuation, and spread money across schemes or combine them with large REITs.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. Schemes and platforms named are examples, not recommendations. Projected yields are not guaranteed, SM REIT rules continue to evolve, and details may have changed since publication. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a tax professional before investing.
